final.title: When glossary upkeep should stay manual
final.body:
If your glossary only needs a few occasional fixes, keep it manual. AI is not the first move for a low-volume task.

The better question is simple: is glossary upkeep a repeatable workflow, or just a series of one-off edits? If the answer is repeatable, document the rule in plain English before you automate anything. For example: what counts as a new term, what counts as a definition change, and which entries must wait for owner sign-off.

That keeps the build small and the decision human. Bareni works best when the workflow is already digital and the rule can be stated clearly. It does not fit scan-heavy, OCR-dependent work, and paper-based glossary sources are out of scope here.

The practical next step is to write down the current process on one page: source, reviewer, approval point, and where the glossary lives. Then you can see whether the problem is real workflow friction or just tidy-up work wearing a business hat.

final.title: When glossary upkeep should stop being manual
final.body:
If glossary upkeep is eating into your week, treat it as a workflow decision, not a vague content problem.

For a small business, the question is simple: are you making the same glossary judgment over and over, or is each update a one-off? If the terms repeat, the source is already digital, and a human can still approve the final change, that is a bounded place to test AI assistance. If the work is rare, messy, or scan-heavy, manual handling is still the better fit. Bareni currently declines scan-heavy, OCR-dependent workflows, so paper-based glossary sources are out of scope.

The next step is to write down the rule in plain English: what counts as a new term, what counts as a definition change, and which changes must wait for owner sign-off before publication. That gives you a clean boundary for deciding whether the task is still a manual job or ready for a small pilot.

No drama. Just a clearer line between upkeep and overkill.
